title: Randomized competitiveness of k-server
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as \(k\to \infty , R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)=\inf\){\(r\ge 1\): for every finite metric \((X,d)\) with |\(X|\ge k+1\) and every initial placement, some randomized online strategy and finite \(\beta \ge 0\) satisfy \(E[\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma )]\le r\cdot \operatorname{OPT}(\sigma )+\beta\) for every finite request sequence \(\sigma\) fixed independently of the strategy’s coins}, for integers \(k\ge 2\).
definitions: There are k movable servers at points of X; repeated server locations are allowed. Each request names a point of X. Before the next request, at least one server must occupy that point. Moving a server from u to v costs \(d(u,v)\). The full finite metric and initial placement are known. \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma )\) is the minimum total movement of a strategy knowing the entire sequence and starting at the same placement. The adversary is oblivious: it fixes \(\sigma\) independently of the online strategy’s random coins. The strategy uses only the prefix revealed so far. No running-time bound is imposed. The competitive factor r is uniform over metric spaces and initial placements for each fixed k. The strategy and additive \(\beta\) may depend on the metric, initial placement, k and r, but not on the future sequence or its length. The infimum is finite by deterministic competitive strategies, and need not be attained.

context_blocks.text: This quantitative target asks for the growth of the optimal competitive ratio. The earlier polylogarithmic question asks only whether that growth is bounded by some fixed power of log k.

Randomized k-server is a central test of whether an online algorithm can manage a large changing state at a cost depending mildly on the number of servers. The number of metric points must not occur in the competitive ratio.
The old \(O(\log  k)\) conjecture is false: a superlogarithmic lower bound is known. Polylogarithmic dependence on k remains a different open target. Bounds containing log|X| do not settle it.

why: A surviving central problem in randomized competitive analysis, beyond the refuted logarithmic k-server conjecture.
answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(f(k)\) and universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) with \(c f(k)\le R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)\le C f(k)\) for all \(k\ge 2\), adjusting constants for finitely many small k if needed, and prove both inequalities in Lean. Upper bounds must hold for every finite metric and oblivious sequence in the stated model; lower bounds must apply to every eligible randomized strategy on suitable metrics. The asymptotic precision is constant-factor matching, not additive 0.01.

progress.text: The 2026 work gives \(O(\log ^{2} k)\) on hierarchical tree metrics and an \(O(\log |X| \log ^{2} k)\) consequence on general metrics; it does not remove dependence on |X|.
An \(\Omega (\log ^{2} k)\) lower bound refutes the original logarithmic conjecture; it is consistent with a polylogarithmic upper bound.

sentences: In randomized k-server, an online strategy moves k servers to serve sequential metric requests.
The request sequence is fixed independently of the strategy’s random choices.
The target is the infimum competitive ratio as a function of k over all finite metrics, within universal constant factors.
The metric and initial placement are known and may affect the strategy and fixed additive cost.
The earlier polylogarithmic question is a qualitative consequence of determining this growth, and dependence on the number of metric points cannot be hidden in the ratio.
